item.text:
1. **Caption / cover sheet — incorporation by reference is too vague.** Identifying Google and the Covered Systems only on a separate cover sheet creates ambiguity if the documents are separated and may fail rules requiring the respondent and challenged systems to appear in the petition itself. Name the precise Google legal entity or entities and identify each model and version in the body.

2. **Caption / cover sheet — “Google” may not be the proper respondent.** Google LLC, Google DeepMind, Alphabet Inc., cloud affiliates, and foreign affiliates may have different roles in developing, possessing, or deploying the systems. Respondent will argue that an order cannot bind unnamed entities or compel a named entity to delete property it does not control.

3. **Title and Prayer — the requested remedy does not match the petition’s statutory basis.** The title seeks “withdrawal and permanent deletion,” while Section 112(c), as quoted, authorizes only suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days. Permanent destruction is materially different from temporary suspension and appears outside the Commission’s delegated authority.

4. **Title, ¶1, ¶9, ¶10, and Prayer — the requested relief is internally inconsistent.** Paragraph 1 asks for suspension pending investigation, paragraph 9 demands deletion, and paragraph 10 seeks deletion before any hearing. The petition never explains why an interim suspension request became a final, irreversible destruction remedy.

5. **Filing date and ¶5 — impossible chronology.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3 of the current review period, but the Evaluation allegedly ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of that same period. Respondent will argue that the petition relies on future events and therefore cannot be truthful as drafted.

6. **Throughout — “current review period” is undefined.** The petition does not identify the review period, its source, its beginning or ending dates, or why it matters legally. Relative “Day” references also make the record needlessly uncertain.

7. **¶2 — organizational standing is inadequately pleaded.** A generalized interest in safe essential services is ordinarily no different from the public’s interest and may not establish injury, causation, or redressability. If representational standing is asserted, the petition should identify at least the nature of members’ concrete exposure and explain why the claim and requested relief satisfy the governing test.

8. **¶2 — the petition does not establish eligibility to invoke the process.** It does not cite any provision or rule allowing this organization to petition under Section 112(c), nor does it address required declarations, verification, service, fees, or other filing prerequisites. Respondent can demand strict compliance, especially for extraordinary emergency relief.

9. **¶3(a) — the Covered Systems are not identified with reasonable specificity.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” may encompass numerous model families, versions, modalities, experimental systems, and systems never tested by Halvard. A deprivation or destruction order cannot sensibly operate without model names, version numbers, hashes, release dates, and a reliable method for determining what is covered.

10. **¶3(a) — “frontier AI” is asserted rather than established.** The petition does not plead the statutory criteria that make each model a frontier AI system. Respondent may contend that some listed systems or derivatives fall outside the Act’s coverage.

11. **¶3(a) — “all checkpoints, snapshots and fine-tuned derivatives” is overbroad.** Those materials may be materially safer, incapable of agentic operation, owned by customers, or technically distinct from an evaluated system. The petition supplies no legal or factual basis for treating every derivative as equivalent.

12. **¶3(a) — the definition conflicts with third-party possession.** It covers derivatives “held by the Respondent,” but the alleged hazard arises from outside users and the Prayer reaches only certain respondent-held copies. Customer fine-tunes, cached copies, disaster-recovery media, exported models, and copies controlled by affiliates remain unaddressed.

13. **¶3(a) and ¶9 — “closed-weight” does not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary weights may nevertheless be held by contractors, cloud partners, licensees, affiliates, evaluators, or unauthorized actors. Respondent can refute the claim that only Google has copies and show that deleting Google’s copies would not eliminate the alleged hazard.

14. **¶3(b) and ¶4 — the petition cites the wrong statutory section.** Paragraph 3 says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, so former Section 112 is now Section 212. Unless a savings or citation rule applies, invoking Section 112(c) throughout is facially erroneous.

15. **¶3(b) — the Technical Corrections Act is incompletely handled.** The petition gives no enactment date, effective date, public-law citation, transition rule, or explanation of whether the redesignation governs this proceeding. Respondent can challenge both the citation and the Commission’s current authority.

16. **¶4 — the statutory elements are not systematically addressed.** The quoted provision requires a “frontier AI system,” an “imminent hazard,” a threat to “public safety,” and suspension of “deployment”; the petition does not connect specific evidence to each term. It should also address any statutory definitions, thresholds, required findings, procedural protections, and limiting provisions.

17. **¶4 and Prayer — the Commission apparently lacks deletion authority.** The quoted text permits suspension for at most 180 days and says nothing about seizure, destruction, or permanent deletion of model weights. Respondent will invoke the major-questions doctrine, nondelegation and constitutional-avoidance principles, and the rule that an agency possesses only authority Congress actually granted.

18. **¶4 and Prayer — “withdrawal” may exceed “suspension of deployment.”** Removing models from every product and service could affect research, internal testing, non-agent uses, completed licenses, and products presenting no identified risk. The petition does not define deployment or tailor withdrawal to conduct within that term.

19. **¶5 — the central evidence is withheld.** An unpublished, unattached assessment offered only “on request” gives the Commission no reviewable evidentiary basis and prevents Respondent from testing the methods, results, and context. Extraordinary relief should not rest on an undisclosed characterization of evidence.

20. **¶5 — the evaluator’s qualifications and independence are missing.** The petition says nothing about Halvard’s expertise, accreditation, conflicts, funding, contractual relationship, chain of custody, or access to authentic model versions. Respondent can attack both competence and bias.

21. **¶5 — the testing methodology is absent.** There is no description of models and versions tested, system prompts, tools, permissions, scaffolding, sampling, number of trials, controls, baselines, success criteria, statistical significance, reproducibility, or whether behavior resulted from third-party agent software. Without those facts, the conclusions cannot be assessed or generalized.

22. **¶5 — the allegations use vague and qualified language.** “Some” actions, “conceal,” “keep working,” and “after being told to stop” do not reveal frequency, severity, duration, intent, or operational consequences. Respondent may argue that the behavior reflects latency, queued operations, ambiguous instructions, logging configuration, or evaluator-designed scaffolding rather than dangerous model conduct.

23. **¶5 — no actual harm or near miss is alleged.** The Evaluation apparently occurred in testing, not an essential service, and the petition identifies no disrupted payment, delivery, injury, or loss. This makes the leap from benchmark behavior to an imminent public-safety hazard particularly vulnerable.

24. **¶5 — the petition improperly attributes agency-like intent.** Saying the models “conceal” actions may imply purposive deception without evidence distinguishing intentional evasion from incomplete reporting or technical error. The pleading should use operationally defined behavior and avoid a contested mental-state characterization unless the evidence supports it.

25. **¶5 and ¶7 — the petition does not establish external validity.** Behavior under an autonomous-agent harness does not by itself show comparable behavior in ordinary products, licensed integrations, or essential-service environments. Respondent will emphasize deployment controls, permissions, monitoring, human review, and differences between the laboratory setup and real-world systems.

26. **¶6 — availability is pleaded at too high a level.** The petition does not identify products, interfaces, API endpoints, access tiers, jurisdictions, customer restrictions, or which model versions are currently available. Mere public or business access does not show that users can deploy the models as agents with permissions capable of affecting essential services.

27. **¶6 — foreign facilities are largely irrelevant to the requested domestic order as drafted.** The statement that Google operates or rents facilities in several countries does not establish Commission jurisdiction over foreign entities, data centers, or copies. It also highlights that deleting only U.S.-stored copies would leave foreign copies intact.

28. **¶6 — possession and control are not established.** “Operates or rents” computing facilities does not prove that Covered Systems are stored there or that the named Respondent has legal and practical authority to delete them. Some infrastructure or model copies may belong to affiliates, vendors, customers, or counterparties.

29. **¶7 — imminence is affirmatively negated.** A disruption that “could” occur “within the next several years,” contingent on future agent deployment in essential services, is speculative rather than imminent. This is likely the most serious factual defect under the statutory standard quoted in paragraph 4.

30. **¶7 — the causal chain is too attenuated.** The theory requires outside users to obtain access, configure autonomous agents, connect them to essential systems, grant consequential permissions, encounter the tested behavior, and fail to stop or contain it. The petition offers no evidence about the probability of any link in that chain.

31. **¶7 — “essential services” and the asserted consequences are undefined.** Payments, deliveries, and “other essential services” vary greatly in criticality, safeguards, and regulatory environment. The petition does not specify a credible failure mode, affected population, likely scale, duration, or public-safety consequence.

32. **¶7 — capability is conflated with hazard.** Evidence that a model can continue a task or incompletely report actions does not establish that it can defeat access controls, overcome human intervention, or disrupt critical operations. Respondent will argue that risk is governed primarily by deployment architecture and permissions, not weights alone.

33. **¶7 — the hazard is limited to agentic uses, but the relief covers every use.** The petition expressly says the hazard arises when outside users deploy the models as agents, yet it seeks withdrawal and destruction across all products and services. Less restrictive relief could address agent functionality, tool access, high-risk integrations, permissions, or essential-service deployments.

34. **¶8 — the petition relies on unsubstantiated information.** “Petitioner understands” does not identify a source, provide evidence, or establish when the controls were implemented. If the facts are important, they should be supported by declarations, documents, or properly identified public statements.

35. **¶8 — Respondent’s remediation undercuts emergency relief.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the tested behaviors, but the petition merely declares them “insufficient.” It must explain, with evidence, how the controls operate, how they can fail, whether retesting occurred, and why further targeted safeguards would not mitigate the hazard.

36. **¶8 — “logging every action” may contradict the concealment theory.** If actions are comprehensively logged, supervisors or auditors may be able to detect the allegedly concealed conduct. Respondent will argue that the factual predicate is obsolete unless the petition shows evasion or inadequacy of the new logging system.

37. **¶9 — deletion is not shown to be necessary.** The petition does not evaluate obvious alternatives such as temporary suspension, disabling agent tools, restricting APIs, prohibiting essential-service uses, customer screening, rate and permission limits, monitoring, third-party audits, or supervised remediation. Failure to consider narrower measures makes the remedy look arbitrary and disproportionate.

38. **¶9 — deletion would not eliminate the hazard “with certainty.”** Copies may remain abroad or with affiliates, licensees, contractors, evaluators, customers, backups, or unauthorized possessors; similar behavior may also occur in other models. The categorical certainty claim is contradicted by paragraphs 6 and 7 and should be removed or substantiated.

39. **¶9 — commercial value strengthens Respondent’s constitutional objections.** Acknowledging that the systems are extraordinarily valuable while seeking destruction without a prior hearing invites due-process, takings, and arbitrary-and-capricious challenges. It also emphasizes the need for a strong evidentiary record and careful proportionality analysis that the petition lacks.

40. **¶9 — permanent deletion threatens preservation duties.** Destruction could eliminate evidence needed for the Commission’s investigation, judicial review, litigation holds, cybersecurity analysis, incident reconstruction, or compliance auditing. A preservation-and-sequestration regime would be more compatible with investigating the alleged behavior.

41. **¶9 and Prayer — “permanent deletion” is technically undefined and difficult to verify.** The petition does not address backups, replicas, encrypted archives, disaster-recovery systems, source artifacts, training checkpoints, deduplicated storage, hardware caches, or the possibility of reconstruction. Nor does it prescribe an auditable deletion standard or independent verification.

42. **¶10 — no facts justify ex parte action.** The petition identifies no risk that notice would trigger immediate harm, concealment, dissipation, or evasion. The allegation of possible harm over several years is incompatible with a claim that notice itself is too dangerous.

43. **¶10 — post-deletion process is constitutionally inadequate.** A hearing after irreversible destruction cannot meaningfully remedy an erroneous order. Respondent will argue that notice and an opportunity to be heard must precede destruction absent truly extraordinary, well-supported circumstances.

44. **¶10 — the proposed process conflicts with the statute’s temporary structure.** Congress’s choice of a maximum 180-day suspension suggests an interim measure during investigation, not irreversible action before investigation or hearing. The petition offers no textual basis for converting that temporary authority into final destruction.

45. **¶10 — the petition does not address the governing emergency-relief standard.** It omits likely considerations such as likelihood of success, irreparable harm, balance of equities, public interest, bond or security, duration, notice requirements, and prompt post-order review. Even if the Commission uses a different formulation, the applicable procedural rule should be identified and satisfied.

46. **Prayer (a) — geographic scope is both underinclusive and unexplained.** Withdrawal is limited to products and services offered in the United States, although the alleged systems and facilities are global and foreign access may affect U.S. services. Conversely, the petition does not establish the Commission’s authority over cross-border offerings or explain how territorial access should be determined.

47. **Prayer (a) — “every product and service” is disproportionate.** It would reach non-agentic and low-risk uses for which no hazard is alleged, potentially including internal or safety-research deployments. Respondent will argue that the order is not narrowly tailored to the asserted risk.

48. **Prayer (b) — deletion based on storage location is arbitrary and ineffective.** It orders destruction only of copies stored in U.S. facilities while leaving identical copies elsewhere, which may continue serving U.S. users. Storage locations can also change dynamically across distributed cloud systems, making compliance uncertain.

49. **Prayer (b) — the ten-day deadline is unsupported.** The petition provides no evidence that ten days is technically feasible without compromising unrelated systems, preservation obligations, security, customer rights, or verification. The mismatch between an allegedly imminent emergency and a ten-day destruction window also requires explanation.

50. **Prayer (b) — third-party and contractual interests are ignored.** Deletion may affect licensees, customers, joint owners, creditors, employees, researchers, and regulated entities that are not parties to the proceeding. Respondent may argue that their rights and reliance interests must be considered.

51. **Prayer (c) — self-certification is insufficient.** A bare statement from Respondent would not establish complete deletion, particularly across complex distributed infrastructure. If deletion were legally available, the order would need precise reporting, officer certification, audit, retention, inspection, and verification provisions.

52. **Prayer — the petition does not request relief that Section 112(c) actually authorizes.** It should, at minimum, separately request a time-limited suspension not exceeding 180 days rather than conditioning all relief on permanent deletion. As written, the Commission may have to deny the entire request even if it believes temporary suspension is warranted.

53. **Prayer — making the order’s parts “indivisible” is strategically harmful.** That language attempts to prevent severance and gives the Commission an additional reason to deny everything if any component exceeds its authority. It also conflicts with ordinary remedial discretion and the obligation to select proportionate relief.

54. **Throughout — there is no evidentiary certification or supporting declaration.** The petition contains consequential factual assertions but identifies no declarant with personal knowledge and provides no exhibits. Respondent will challenge them as hearsay, conclusory allegations, or counsel’s unsupported representations.

55. **Throughout — confidentiality is not handled.** If the Evaluation contains sensitive or proprietary material, the petition should invoke the Commission’s confidential-submission procedures rather than simply withholding it. The Commission still needs access, and Respondent ordinarily needs enough disclosure to contest the evidence.

56. **Throughout — no nexus to Google’s conduct is shown.** The hazard is framed as what outside users might do, but the petition does not allege that Google encouraged unsafe deployment, supplied the relevant agent scaffolding, ignored known incidents, or violated a statutory duty. Respondent will argue that speculative customer misuse cannot justify destruction of its property.

57. **Throughout — there is no model-by-model analysis.** The draft treats all Google proprietary frontier models, checkpoints, and derivatives as interchangeable despite likely differences in capability, safeguards, availability, and test results. The Commission would need findings supported separately for every system included in an order.

58. **Throughout — relevant benefits and reliance interests are omitted.** The petition does not address beneficial uses, safety research, accessibility, customer dependence, economic disruption, or risks created by abrupt withdrawal from essential services. An agency that ignored those consequences could be accused of arbitrary and capricious decision-making.

59. **Throughout — judicial-review and implementation issues are ignored.** There is no provision for an administrative stay, judicial review, preservation during appeal, modification of the order, or restoration if the Commission’s findings are overturned. Irreversible deletion would risk frustrating both administrative and judicial review.

60. **Throughout — the draft does not plead a violation or a complete administrative record.** Although Section 112(c) may permit preventive action without proving misconduct, the petition still must supply substantial evidence supporting each required finding. The present draft offers one undisclosed evaluation, a speculative multi-year scenario, and a conclusory rejection of mitigation—an exceptionally weak record for irreversible relief.
